hypotheses.observation: The structural operator covers 0.42 of measured target-local workload and has a derived candidate speedup upper bound of 1.30, while the micro operator covers only 0.002 despite an 8.0x candidate speedup.
hypotheses.mechanism: Amdahl-style limiting behavior makes the larger covered fraction more influential; the micro operator's small scope limits end-to-end impact.
hypotheses.transformation: Prioritize investigating the structural transformation in the dominant block-level data path; defer the micro-kernel transformation.
preconditions: The measured local workload is representative of the deployment workload.
The 1.30 structural speedup bound is achievable without offsetting overhead.
hypotheses.expected_effect: The structural candidate has an estimated end-to-end upper-bound improvement of about 9.8% for the stated local fraction, versus about 0.2% for the micro candidate.
risks: The derived speedup is only an upper bound.
The measured local workload fraction may not represent deployment mix.
Transformation overhead or resource effects may reduce the realized benefit.
unknowns: Deployment workload mix is not measured.
Realized speedups and overheads are unknown.
required_evidence: Benchmark the transformed structural path including overhead and end-to-end runtime.

hypotheses.observation: The two candidates touch disjoint execution regions, so their effects may be composable, but both supplied speedups are only derived upper bounds.
hypotheses.mechanism: Disjoint regions reduce direct transformation interference, while total benefit remains constrained by the unchanged workload and by each candidate's realized speedup.
hypotheses.transformation: Evaluate the structural candidate first, then measure whether adding the micro-kernel transformation provides a measurable incremental benefit.
preconditions: The regions remain disjoint in the implemented configuration.
The structural transformation does not alter the micro-kernel's workload or costs.
Both transformations preserve correctness and fit resource limits.
hypotheses.expected_effect: The combined upper-bound benefit is dominated by the structural candidate; the micro transformation is expected to add only a small incremental improvement relative to it.
risks: Disjoint source regions may still share memory, bandwidth, synchronization, or resource limits.
The micro candidate may add complexity without meaningful end-to-end gain.
unknowns: Whether implementation overhead couples the regions.
Whether the combined transformations change occupancy, bandwidth, or scheduling.
required_evidence: Measure end-to-end runtime for structural-only and structural-plus-micro variants.
Measure resource utilization and verify no cross-region interference.

hypotheses.observation: The recorded fractions apply to the target local workload, but deployment mix is explicitly unmeasured.
hypotheses.mechanism: A transformation that is valuable for the local workload may have a different system-level value when the local workload is weighted differently in deployment.
hypotheses.transformation: Conduct workload-mix measurement before making a system-level prioritization or promotion decision.
preconditions: Representative deployment traces or workload samples are available.
The target local workload can be identified consistently in those samples.
hypotheses.expected_effect: The measurement will distinguish whether the structural candidate's local advantage translates to deployment-level benefit and whether the micro candidate is worth pursuing.
risks: A narrow or unrepresentative trace can misestimate deployment value.
Mix measurement alone does not establish transformation correctness or realized speedup.
unknowns: Deployment frequency and time share of the target local workload.
Deployment-level end-to-end impact of either candidate.
required_evidence: Collect representative deployment workload traces and quantify target-local workload share.
Validate candidate speedups with end-to-end measurements on that mix.
